outputs.desc: Payload capacity reduction from expendable mode due to landing propellant reserve

process: RTLS (return to launch site): requires a boostback burn to reverse the downrange velocity. For a stage separating at Mach 6-10, the boostback delta-v is 1,000-2,000 m/s. Then an entry burn at the atmosphere interface (300-600 m/s) to reduce heating and loads, then a landing burn (300-500 m/s). Total return delta-v: 1,500-3,000 m/s. Payload penalty: 30-50%.

ASDS (autonomous spaceport droneship): the stage continues downrange and lands on a floating platform. No boostback needed. Entry burn and landing burn only. Total return delta-v: 500-1,200 m/s. Payload penalty: 15-30%. Used for high-energy missions where RTLS costs too much payload.

Landing burn design: the final landing burn starts at 500-1000 m altitude, 200-300 m/s velocity. A single engine (minimum throttle still exceeds 1g for most engines, so the burn must be timed precisely). The hover-slam (suicide burn) starts late and decelerates at >1g to touchdown at near-zero velocity. No hover capability means zero margin for timing error.

Entry burn: fired at approximately 70 km altitude and Mach 5-8 to create a virtual shock ahead of the vehicle, reducing aerodynamic heating and loads on the engine section. Burns for 15-20 seconds using 3 engines. Without this burn, the engine bells and octaweb would be damaged by reentry heating.

The payload penalty is the cost of reusability in performance. Calculate by comparing propellant mass budgeted for return against the rocket equation: each kg of landing propellant reduces payload by the inverse of the payload fraction. A vehicle with 2% payload fraction loses 50 kg of payload per kg of return propellant.

steps.description: Design the landing legs, grid fins, and other hardware needed for controlled descent and landing.

inputs.name: stage-mass-estimates
inputs.desc: Landing mass (dry stage + residual propellant)

inputs.name: landing-trajectory-profile
inputs.desc: Touchdown velocity and attitude requirements

inputs.name: vehicle-geometry
inputs.desc: Stage diameter and height for stability analysis

outputs.name: landing-leg-design
outputs.desc: Leg geometry, material, deployment mechanism, and crush core specification

outputs.name: grid-fin-design
outputs.desc: Grid fin size, material, and actuation system for aerodynamic steering

outputs.name: landing-stability-analysis
outputs.desc: Tip-over analysis for wind, slope, and CG offset

process: Landing legs must absorb the kinetic energy at touchdown (typically 1-3 m/s vertical, 0-2 m/s horizontal). Energy absorption: crushable aluminum honeycomb in the leg strut. The crush stroke must absorb 0.5 * m * v^2 at a force below the structural limit of the vehicle. Typical stroke: 0.2-0.5 m.

Leg geometry: 4 legs gives a square footprint (simple, light, but sensitive to CG offset and slope). Falcon 9 uses 4 legs. More legs improve stability but add mass and mechanism complexity. The footprint radius must be large enough to prevent tip-over under worst-case CG offset and wind. Rule of thumb: footprint radius > 0.5 * vehicle height * tan(max_tilt_angle).

Grid fins: lattice-structure aerodynamic surfaces that provide roll, pitch, and yaw control during supersonic and subsonic descent. They work in the wake of the vehicle (fins at the top of a descending stage). Titanium grid fins survive the high heating during reentry without thermal protection. Sized from the required control moment at the worst-case dynamic pressure.

Cold gas or hydraulic actuation for grid fins. Falcon 9 initially used hydraulic fluid (limited supply = limited steering time); later switched to electric actuators powered by batteries. The actuator rate and authority must handle the guidance commands through transonic flight where aerodynamic characteristics change rapidly.

Deployment sequence: grid fins deploy after stage separation (or remain deployed throughout, as on Falcon 9 Block 5). Landing legs deploy shortly before landing burn ignition. Deployment reliability must be extremely high (legs or fins failing to deploy = loss of vehicle). Redundant mechanisms and positive locking are required.

steps.description: Manage engine life for reuse: track life-limited parts, predict remaining life, and define refurbishment scope.

inputs.name: engine-design-specs
inputs.desc: Engine operating conditions (chamber pressure, temperature, speed)

inputs.name: flight-history
inputs.desc: Number of flights and burn time per flight

inputs.name: inspection-data
inputs.desc: Results from post-flight inspections of critical components

outputs.name: life-limited-parts-list
outputs.desc: Components with defined life limits and remaining life

outputs.name: refurbishment-scope
outputs.desc: What must be inspected, cleaned, replaced, or tested between flights

outputs.name: engine-life-prediction
outputs.desc: Predicted number of flights before major overhaul

process: Life-limited parts in a rocket engine: turbopump bearings (fatigue, wear), turbine blades (creep, thermal fatigue), chamber throat (erosion, thermal cycling), nozzle (thermal fatigue of regenerative cooling channels), injector (erosion, coking), seals (wear, embrittlement). Each has a different failure mechanism and life prediction method.

Turbopump bearing life: ball bearings in cryogenic service degrade from Hertzian contact fatigue. L10 life (90% survival probability) is calculated from load, speed, and material (Si3N4 balls last longer than steel). Target: 20-100 flights per bearing set. Track bearing condition by vibration signature monitoring.

Thermal fatigue of the thrust chamber: each firing cycle (startup to shutdown) cycles the chamber wall from cryogenic (coolant side) to near-melting (gas side). Copper alloy walls develop fatigue cracks in the cooling channels. Life prediction uses strain range from thermal analysis and low-cycle fatigue curves. The SSME chamber liner was replaced every 20-40 flights.

Inspection between flights: borescope inspection of the thrust chamber and turbine, vibration signature analysis of turbopumps, leak checks of all seals and joints, visual inspection of the nozzle and injector face, data review from flight instrumentation. The inspection scope defines the turnaround time (Falcon 9 Block 5 targets less than 24 hours between flights).

Cost of engine refurbishment vs replacement: if refurbishment cost exceeds a threshold fraction of new engine cost (typically 30-50%), replacement is more economical. The goal is to design the engine so that routine maintenance is limited to inspection and replacement of a few low-cost consumable parts (seals, filters, pyrotechnic igniters).

steps.description: Build an economic model comparing reusable and expendable vehicle cost as a function of flight rate, refurbishment cost, and recovery logistics.

inputs.name: vehicle-production-cost
inputs.desc: Cost to manufacture one stage (expendable reference)

inputs.name: refurbishment-scope
inputs.desc: Refurbishment cost per flight

inputs.name: payload-penalty
inputs.desc: Payload reduction from landing propellant reserve

outputs.name: cost-per-flight-vs-reuse-count
outputs.desc: Cost per flight as a function of how many times a stage flies

outputs.name: breakeven-flight-count
outputs.desc: Number of flights per stage where reusable becomes cheaper than expendable

outputs.name: fleet-economics
outputs.desc: Cost model for a fleet of reusable stages at a given annual flight rate

process: Expendable cost per flight: production cost + integration + launch operations. For a Falcon 9-class vehicle, first stage production is roughly 60-70% of total vehicle cost. Upper stage, fairing, and integration are the rest.

Reusable cost per flight: (production cost / number of flights) + refurbishment cost per flight + recovery operations cost. If a stage costs $30M to build, flies 10 times, and costs $2M per refurbishment + $1M recovery: cost per flight = $3M + $2M + $1M = $6M vs $30M expendable. Breakeven at about 3-4 flights.

The learning curve effect: as flight rate increases, production and refurbishment teams become more efficient. Wright's law: each doubling of cumulative production reduces unit cost by 15-20%. At 50+ flights per year, the cost reduction from volume is significant even for expendable vehicles.

Flight rate sensitivity: reusable stages have fixed costs (the stage hardware, amortized) and variable costs (refurbishment, recovery). At low flight rates, the amortized hardware cost per flight is high and reusability may not pay off. At high flight rates, the hardware is nearly free per flight and the variable costs dominate. SpaceX's cost advantage grows with their flight rate.

Payload penalty cost: the customer pays for the payload they need to orbit. If reusability reduces payload capacity by 30%, some missions that fit on an expendable vehicle require a larger (more expensive) reusable vehicle or a two-stage upper stage. Model the customer-facing price to include the payload penalty scenario.

description: Design and execute launch operations: countdown design, launch commit criteria, pad systems, range safety, and post-flight data review.

steps.description: Design the countdown timeline from vehicle rollout through T-0 and liftoff.

inputs.name: vehicle-configuration
inputs.desc: Vehicle type, propellant combination, and ground support requirements

inputs.name: pad-systems-capability
inputs.desc: Ground support equipment capability and constraints

inputs.name: launch-window-schedule
inputs.desc: Available launch window duration and timing

outputs.name: countdown-timeline
outputs.desc: Sequenced timeline of all operations from rollout through T-0

outputs.name: hold-points
outputs.desc: Built-in hold points for verification and go/no-go decisions

outputs.name: recycle-plan
outputs.desc: Procedures for restarting the countdown after a hold or scrub

process: Work backward from T-0: engine ignition and release happens at T-0 or T-3 seconds (after engine health check). Before that: arm flight termination system, switch to internal power, retract umbilicals, final pressurization, terminal countdown sequence (usually automated in the last 30-60 seconds).

Propellant loading: for cryogenic propellants, loading begins T-4 to T-8 hours. LOX is loaded first (denser, lower tank), then fuel (RP-1 can be loaded earlier since it is storable at room temperature). LH2 loading requires continuous topping to replace boiloff. For subcooled/densified propellants (SpaceX), loading occurs late in the countdown (T-35 minutes for Falcon 9).

Chill-down: before engine start, the turbopumps and feed lines must be cooled to cryogenic temperature to prevent cavitation and thermal shock. Chill-down uses propellant bleed through the engine and lasts 5-30 minutes depending on engine design. Engine conditioning sets the thermal state for reliable ignition.

Built-in holds: T-60 minutes (range verification), T-20 minutes (final weather check), T-10 minutes (go/no-go poll of all console positions), T-4 minutes (entering terminal count, autosequence start). Holds pause the countdown clock; operations that are time-sensitive (like cryogenic loading) continue during holds.

Scrub and recycle: if the countdown is stopped after propellant loading, the vehicle must be detanked (propellant drained and tanks safed). Detanking takes 2-6 hours. The turnaround to the next attempt depends on the scrub reason, propellant availability, and launch window. A 24-hour recycle is typical for weather scrubs.

steps.description: Define the go/no-go criteria that must be met for launch to proceed.

inputs.name: vehicle-configuration
inputs.desc: Vehicle systems and their health monitoring capability

inputs.name: launch-site
inputs.desc: Launch site weather patterns and range constraints

inputs.name: mission-requirements
inputs.desc: Mission-specific constraints (crew safety, payload sensitivity)

outputs.name: weather-criteria
outputs.desc: Wind, precipitation, lightning, and cloud ceiling limits for launch

outputs.name: vehicle-health-criteria
outputs.desc: Redline parameters and their limits for each vehicle system

outputs.name: range-criteria
outputs.desc: Range safety requirements that must be met (tracking, FTS, exclusion zones)

process: Weather criteria: surface wind speed (typically <30 knots), upper-level wind shear (from weather balloon soundings, compared to vehicle structural limits), cumulus cloud rules (no launch through or near cumulus with tops above freezing level, to avoid triggered lightning), precipitation, temperature limits for propellant and electronics.

Lightning rules: the most complex weather criteria. Natural lightning within 10 nm in the last 30 minutes = no launch. Triggered lightning risk assessment from electric field mills on the pad and aloft. The vehicle and its exhaust plume can trigger lightning by creating a conducting path through a charge field. Atlas-Centaur 67 was destroyed by triggered lightning.

Vehicle health: every critical system has redline parameters monitored in real time. Engine parameters (pump inlet pressure, turbopump speed, temperatures), tank pressures, battery voltage, IMU alignment quality, flight computer status. Any single redline violation triggers an automatic hold or cutoff.

Range safety requirements: the flight termination system (FTS) must be armed and tested. Tracking systems (radar, telemetry) must be operational. Impact prediction must show the vehicle debris footprint is within the approved corridor. Ship and aircraft exclusion zones must be clear. The range safety officer must have communications with the launch team.

Go/no-go poll: each console position (propulsion, avionics, guidance, range safety, weather, payload, launch director) reports status. Any single 'no-go' stops the count. The launch director makes the final decision. For crewed missions, the crew also has a go/no-go input.

steps.description: Design the launch pad systems: flame deflector, sound suppression, umbilicals, and strongback.

inputs.name: vehicle-configuration
inputs.desc: Vehicle size, thrust, and propellant types

inputs.name: launch-site
inputs.desc: Pad location and existing infrastructure

inputs.name: turnaround-requirement
inputs.desc: Time between launches for multi-mission capability

outputs.name: flame-deflector-design
outputs.desc: Deflector geometry, water flow rate, and material specification

outputs.name: umbilical-system
outputs.desc: Fluid, electrical, and data connections between pad and vehicle

outputs.name: launch-mount-design
outputs.desc: Hold-down and release mechanism specification

outputs.name: sound-suppression-system
outputs.desc: Water deluge system flow rate and nozzle layout

process: Flame deflector: redirects the engine exhaust away from the vehicle. A flame trench with a deflector surface (wedge or bucket shape) directs the exhaust horizontally. The deflector surface must withstand exhaust temperatures (3,000+ K) and velocities (2,000+ m/s). Refractory concrete over steel, with water cooling. The flame trench for a heavy-lift vehicle is typically 10-20 m deep.

Sound suppression water deluge: acoustic energy from the rocket exhaust at launch can damage the vehicle and payload (140-180 dB at the pad). Water injected into the exhaust plume at and just after ignition absorbs acoustic energy. Flow rates of 100,000-1,000,000 liters per minute are typical. The water system must start before engine ignition and continue through liftoff.

Umbilicals: provide propellant, pressurant gas, electrical power, data, and conditioning (air or nitrogen purge for payload fairing) to the vehicle while on the pad. At T-0 or shortly before, umbilicals disconnect. Quick-disconnect fittings must separate cleanly and retract away from the vehicle. A hung umbilical (one that fails to disconnect) can damage the vehicle or pull it off course.

The strongback or erector: supports the vehicle during pad operations, provides access for personnel, and retracts at launch. For a vehicle erected vertically on the pad, the strongback holds the vehicle against wind loads and provides alignment. At T-0, the strongback releases and retracts (SpaceX Falcon 9 strongback retracts just before launch; some designs fall back).

Hold-down and release: the vehicle is held on the pad during engine start and health check (T-3 to T-0). Explosive bolts or hydraulic release clamps. The hold-down force must exceed the maximum engine thrust during the health check. Release must be nearly simultaneous at all hold-down points (within milliseconds) to avoid lateral forces on the vehicle.

steps.description: Design the flight termination system and range safety architecture for public protection.

inputs.name: trajectory-design
inputs.desc: Nominal trajectory and failure mode trajectories

inputs.name: launch-site
inputs.desc: Populated areas and exclusion zones near the flight path

inputs.name: vehicle-configuration
inputs.desc: Vehicle characteristics affecting debris dispersion

outputs.name: fts-design
outputs.desc: Flight termination system architecture (command destruct, AFTS, or both)

outputs.name: destruct-criteria
outputs.desc: Criteria for commanding vehicle destruct (IIP lines, corridor violations)

outputs.name: debris-footprint-analysis
outputs.desc: Predicted debris impact area for nominal and failure cases

outputs.name: casualty-expectation
outputs.desc: Expected casualties from debris (must be below 30 in a million per mission)

process: The flight termination system (FTS) is a safety system that destroys the vehicle if it deviates from the planned trajectory and threatens populated areas. Required by the FAA (14 CFR 450) and the Eastern/Western Range. The range safety officer (RSO) or an autonomous system commands termination.

Command destruct: ground-based radar tracks the vehicle. If the instantaneous impact point (IIP) crosses a destruct line (boundary protecting populated areas), the RSO commands destruct via encrypted radio link. The vehicle's linear shaped charges (LSCs) cut the propellant tanks, dispersing propellant and ending thrust. Two independent FTS receivers and batteries are required.

Autonomous Flight Termination System (AFTS): the vehicle carries its own GPS receiver and pre-loaded trajectory corridor. If the vehicle exits the corridor, the on-board computer commands termination automatically. AFTS eliminates dependence on ground tracking infrastructure and enables launches from sites without full range support. SpaceX, ULA, and others now use AFTS.

Debris analysis: model the vehicle breakup (from FTS or failure) and propagate debris trajectories through the atmosphere to impact. Consider aerodynamic drag on each fragment, wind, and fragment mass distribution. The debris footprint is an ellipse oriented along the wind direction, typically 5-20 km long.

Casualty expectation (Ec): Ec = sum over all populated areas of (probability of debris reaching area * population density * casualty area per fragment). FAA requires Ec < 30 per million per mission for each individual and collective risk. This analysis drives the destruct corridor boundaries and may restrict launch times based on ship and aircraft traffic.

steps.description: Conduct the post-flight data review to verify vehicle performance, identify anomalies, and certify for next flight.

inputs.name: flight-telemetry
inputs.desc: Complete telemetry dataset from the flight

inputs.name: vehicle-configuration
inputs.desc: As-flown vehicle configuration and predicted performance

inputs.name: inspection-data
inputs.desc: Post-flight hardware inspection results (for reusable stages)

outputs.name: flight-performance-assessment
outputs.desc: Actual vs predicted performance for every subsystem

outputs.name: anomaly-list
outputs.desc: All anomalies identified during flight with severity and root cause assessment

outputs.name: flight-readiness-for-next-mission
outputs.desc: Certification that the vehicle design is ready for the next flight

process: Reconstruct the trajectory: compare actual position, velocity, and attitude from navigation data with the predicted trajectory. Differences indicate performance variations (engine Isp, drag, wind) or anomalies. The reconstructed trajectory is the ground truth for all subsequent analysis.

Engine performance: compare measured chamber pressure, turbopump speeds, temperatures, and mixture ratio with predictions. Calculate actual Isp and thrust from chamber pressure and flow rates. Any deviation from prediction is investigated. Engine performance data feeds the model for the next flight prediction.

GNC performance: evaluate navigation accuracy (comparing INS solution with GPS if available), guidance commanding, and control system response. Check control actuator usage (gimbal angles, RCS pulses) against predictions. Excessive control activity may indicate unexpected disturbances or model errors.

Structural loads: compare measured accelerations, acoustic environment, and temperatures with the design loads analysis. If any measurement exceeds the predicted envelope, investigate whether the structure was overloaded and whether the design loads analysis needs updating.

Anomaly resolution: each anomaly is categorized by severity (critical, major, minor) and assigned a root cause investigation team. No anomaly may be carried forward to the next flight without either a root cause and corrective action, or a formal risk acceptance by the mission assurance authority. This process is the final gate before the next launch.
